claim: Maternal spindle transfer (MST) overcomes massive embryo developmental arrest characteristic of non-manipulated NZB oocytes by replacing the entire cytoplasm with B6CBAF1 cytoplasm.
source: Our proof-of-concept experiments show that replacement of the entire cytoplasm of oocytes from a sensitive mouse strain overcomes massive embryo developmental arrest characteristic of non-manipulated oocytes.
evidence: The abstract states that replacement of entire cytoplasm overcomes developmental arrest, and this is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Table 2 demonstrating 10-fold increase in blastocyst formation.

claim: MST results in minimal carryover of mtDNA following the procedure.
source: Genetic analysis confirmed minimal carryover of mtDNA following MST.
evidence: Confirmed by sequencing data in Figure 3 showing mean heteroplasmy levels below 2.9% in embryos and Figure 4 showing levels of 2.3 ± 1.3% in F1 adult mice.

claim: Mice generated by MST showed low heteroplasmy levels in multiple organs at adult age.
source: Resulting mice showed low heteroplasmy levels in multiple organs at adult age, normal histology and fertility.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4a showing heteroplasmy levels ranging from undetectable to 3.5% across multiple organs in F1 adult mice.

claim: MST-generated mice showed normal histology.
source: Resulting mice showed low heteroplasmy levels in multiple organs at adult age, normal histology and fertility.
evidence: Histological examinations described in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2 revealed no lesions or abnormalities except one control animal.

claim: MST-generated mice showed normal fertility.
source: Resulting mice showed low heteroplasmy levels in multiple organs at adult age, normal histology and fertility.
evidence: Fertility data presented in Supplementary file 4 showing all F1 MST mice were fertile with mean litter size of 7.8 ± 1.4 pups/animal.

claim: Heteroplasmy was reduced in F2 mice compared to F1 mice.
source: Mice were followed for five generations (F5), revealing that heteroplasmy was reduced in F2 mice and was undetectable in the subsequent generations.
evidence: Data in Figure 4c and Supplementary file 5 showing F2 heteroplasmy reduced to 0.4 ± 0.6% compared to F1 at 2.3 ± 1.3%.

claim: Heteroplasmy was undetectable in F3 to F5 generations.
source: Mice were followed for five generations (F5), revealing that heteroplasmy was reduced in F2 mice and was undetectable in the subsequent generations.
evidence: Supplementary file 5 shows undetectable heteroplasmy levels in F3-F5 generations.

claim: Enucleation was successful in 98.9% of B6CBAF1 oocytes.
source: Enucleation was successful in 98.9% of oocytes (n = 790) and reconstruction was achieved in 96.1% (n = 321), confirmed using a microscope with polarized light that allows visualization of the birefringence of the spindle microtubules (Figure 1b–c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement reported in the text with sample size n=790.

claim: Reconstruction was achieved in 96.1% of B6CBAF1 oocytes.
source: Enucleation was successful in 98.9% of oocytes (n = 790) and reconstruction was achieved in 96.1% (n = 321), confirmed using a microscope with polarized light that allows visualization of the birefringence of the spindle microtubules (Figure 1b–c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement reported in the text with sample size n=321.

claim: Vitrified B6CBAF1 oocytes showed 97.7% survival rate after warming.
source: Next, MST was carried out with both fresh and cryopreserved B6CBAF1 oocytes that were vitrified and warmed using the open Cryotop system (97.7% survival, n = 600).
evidence: Direct experimental measurement with sample size n=600.

claim: All MST oocytes analyzed presented a spindle with normal barrel shape and chromosomes aligned at the MII plate regardless of whether fresh or vitrified gametes were used.
source: All oocytes analyzed presented a spindle with a normal barrel shape and with the chromosomes aligned at the MII plate (fresh-sp/fresh-cyt n = 20, fresh-sp/vitrified-cyt n = 15, vitrified-sp/fresh-cyt n = 15, vitrified-sp/vitrified-cyt n = 16; Figure 1e–f), regardless of whether fresh or vitrified gametes were used as spindle or cytoplast donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1e-f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with sample sizes provided for each group.

claim: MST procedures did not induce premature activation of oocytes.
source: Furthermore, there was no evidence that the procedure was inducing premature activation of the oocytes.
evidence: Based on observation of spindle structure and chromosome alignment in fixed oocytes as described in the preceding text.

claim: Oocytes composed of vitrified spindles transferred into vitrified cytoplasts showed significantly lower two-cell development (82.4%) compared to non-manipulated fresh controls (96.8%, p=0.001).
source: Interestingly, a significantly lower proportion of inseminated oocytes composed of vitrified spindles transferred into vitrified cytoplasts (vitrified-sp/vitrified-cyt) developed to the two-cell stage (82.4%, n = 85) compared with non-manipulated fresh (96.8%, n = 94, p=0.001) or vitrified (96.7%, n = 90, p=0.001) controls.
evidence: Statistical comparison of experimental groups with p-values provided, data shown in Figure 1j and Table 1.

claim: When spindles from vitrified oocytes were transferred into fresh cytoplasts, two-cell stage (100%) and blastocyst formation (85.6%) rates were equivalent to fresh controls.
source: On the contrary, when spindles from vitrified oocytes were transferred into fresh cytoplasts (vitrified-sp/fresh-cyt, n = 90), two-cell stage (100%) and blastocyst formation (85.6%) rates were high and equivalent to fresh controls (96.8% and 84.1%, respectively) or to MST oocytes where fresh spindles were transferred into fresh cytoplasts (fresh-st/fresh-cyt, n = 100, 99% and 81%, respectively) (Figure 1j and Table 1).
evidence: Comparative developmental rates across experimental groups shown in Figure 1j and Table 1.

claim: The mean number of total cells in blastocysts from fresh-st/fresh-cyt group (177.8 ± 26.7) was equivalent to controls (192 ± 29.5).
source: Additionally, the mean number of total cells (mean ± SD, n) in the blastocysts obtained in the fresh-st/fresh-cyt group (177.8 ± 26.7, n = 81) was equivalent to controls (192 ± 29.5; n = 79).
evidence: Cell counting data from blastocysts with statistical comparison.

claim: No differences were found in the number of inner cell mass cells positive for Oct4 between fresh-st/fresh-cyt (22.4 ± 3.5) and control groups (25.3 ± 5.6).
source: No differences were found either in the number of inner cell mass cells that were positive for the Oct4 pluripotency marker between fresh-st/fresh-cyt and control groups (22.4 ± 3.5; n = 14 versus 25.3 ± 5.6; n = 10, see also Figure 1i).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of Oct4-positive cells shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Vitrification induces changes that make cryopreserved oocytes unsuitable for use as cytoplasts.
source: Experiments indicate that vitrification induces changes that make cryopreserved oocytes unsuitable for use as cytoplasts.
evidence: Based on the lower developmental rates observed when vitrified cytoplasts were used, as shown in Table 1 and Figure 1j.

claim: The spindle apparatus does not appear to be damaged during vitrification or MST procedures.
source: However, the spindle apparatus does not appear to be damaged during vitrification or MST procedures.
evidence: Based on normal spindle morphology observed in immunofluorescence and equivalent developmental rates when vitrified spindles were used with fresh cytoplasts.

claim: NZB control oocytes presented significantly lower fertilization rates than B6CBAF1 control oocytes.
source: As expected, NZB control oocytes presented significantly lower fertilization rates than B6CBAF1 control oocytes, measured as two-cell stage development (Figure 2b and Table 2).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 2b and Table 2 comparing two-cell development rates between strains.

claim: Blastocyst formation rates were close to 80% (77.8%) in the B6CBAF1 control group.
source: Additionally, while blastocyst formation rates were close to 80% in the B6CBAF1 control group (77.8%, n = 144), most of the injected oocytes from the NZB control group arrested their development before reaching this stage (5.6% developed into blastocysts, n = 159, Figure 2b and Table 2).
evidence: Blastocyst formation data shown in Figure 2b and Table 2.

claim: Most injected oocytes from the NZB control group arrested development before blastocyst stage (5.6% developed into blastocysts).
source: Additionally, while blastocyst formation rates were close to 80% in the B6CBAF1 control group (77.8%, n = 144), most of the injected oocytes from the NZB control group arrested their development before reaching this stage (5.6% developed into blastocysts, n = 159, Figure 2b and Table 2).
evidence: Developmental arrest data shown in Figure 2b and Table 2.

claim: When NZB spindles were transferred into B6CBAF1 cytoplasts, blastocyst formation rates were 10-fold higher (51.4%) compared to non-manipulated NZB control (p<0.0001).
source: Remarkably, when the meiotic spindles from NZB oocytes were transferred into B6CBAF1 cytoplasts (NZB-sp/B6-cyt), the blastocyst formation rates were 10-fold higher (51.4%, n = 212, p<0.0001) compared to the non-manipulated NZB control (Figure 2b and Table 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison with p-value provided, data shown in Figure 2b and Table 2.

claim: When B6CBAF1 spindles were transferred into NZB cytoplasts, no blastocysts were obtained (0%).
source: In the reciprocal MST group, B6CBAF1 spindles transferred into NZB cytoplasts (B6-sp/NZB-cyt), blastocysts were not obtained (0%, n = 110), indicating that cytoplasmic factors are likely to be responsible for the lower fertilisation and massive developmental arrest observed at preimplantation stages in the NZB strain (Figure 2b,c and Table 2).
evidence: Developmental data shown in Figure 2b,c and Table 2.

claim: Cytoplasmic factors are likely responsible for the lower fertilisation and massive developmental arrest observed at preimplantation stages in the NZB strain.
source: In the reciprocal MST group, B6CBAF1 spindles transferred into NZB cytoplasts (B6-sp/NZB-cyt), blastocysts were not obtained (0%, n = 110), indicating that cytoplasmic factors are likely to be responsible for the lower fertilisation and massive developmental arrest observed at preimplantation stages in the NZB strain (Figure 2b,c and Table 2).
evidence: Inference based on reciprocal MST experiments showing that NZB cytoplasm leads to developmental arrest regardless of nuclear genome source.

claim: A total of 65 MST blastocysts from the NZB-sp/B6-cyt group resulted in 14 live pups (21.5%) after transfer.
source: A total of 65 MST blastocysts from the NZB-sp/B6-cyt MST group were then warmed (100% survival) and transferred non-surgically into six recipients, which resulted in 14 live pups (21.5%) (Figure 2d,e and Table 3).
evidence: In vivo developmental data shown in Figure 2d,e and Table 3.

claim: The birth rate from NZB-sp/B6-cyt MST (21.5%) is comparable to B6CBAF1 control group (25.9%).
source: This birth rate is comparable (p>0.05) with results obtained from the B6CBAF1 control group (15 live pups (25.9%) out of 58 blastocysts transferred into five recipients).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference (p>0.05) between groups.

claim: Only six pups developed to term from 44 morulas/blastocysts (13.6%) transferred from the control NZB group.
source: Consistent with expectations, only six pups developed to term from 44 morulas/blastocysts (13.6%) transferred into five recipients from the control NZB group.
evidence: In vivo developmental data from control NZB group.

claim: All living pups from MST were born healthy and respired normally.
source: All living pups were born healthy and respired normally.
evidence: Observational data from pup births.

claim: No significant differences were found in placenta and pup size and weight between MST and control groups at 18.5 dpc.
source: Caesarean sections at 18.5 dpc were performed in two recipients of each group to evaluate the size and weight of the placentas and the corresponding pups, with no significant differences found between groups (Table 4).
evidence: Weight measurements shown in Table 4 with no statistical differences reported.

claim: MST procedures do not typically induce an overgrowth phenotype of the type described for somatic cell nuclear transfer.
source: These results suggest that MST procedures do not typically induce an overgrowth phenotype of the type described for certain other techniques, such as somatic cell nuclear transfer (Costa-Borges et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on normal placenta and pup weights compared to controls, with citation to previous work on SCNT.

claim: The mean variant (NZB) allele frequencies from polar bodies (6.2 ± 6.2%) were significantly higher than in complementary two-cell-stage embryos (0.5 ± 0.8%, p=0.0095).
source: Analysis of mtDNA carryover after MST in biopsied cells and the complementary embryos (Figure 3a), revealed that the mean variant (NZB) allele frequencies obtained from polar bodies were significantly higher compared to the mean frequencies in the complementary two-cell-stage embryos (6.2 ± 6.2% SD versus 0.5 ± 0.8% SD; p=0.0095) (Figure 3b).
evidence: Statistical comparison with p-value provided, data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was no significant difference in mtDNA allele frequencies between biopsied blastomeres and corresponding embryos at cleavage stage.
source: By contrast, there was no significant difference in mtDNA allele frequencies between biopsied blastomeres and trophectoderm samples when compared to the corresponding embryos (cleavage-stage: 1.3 ± 1.0% SD versus 1.9 ± 0.6% SD, respectively; blastocyst stage: 1.7 ± 0.9% SD versus 1.9 ± 0.6% SD, respectively).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference, with data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was no significant difference in mtDNA allele frequencies between trophectoderm biopsies and corresponding embryos at blastocyst stage.
source: By contrast, there was no significant difference in mtDNA allele frequencies between biopsied blastomeres and trophectoderm samples when compared to the corresponding embryos (cleavage-stage: 1.3 ± 1.0% SD versus 1.9 ± 0.6% SD, respectively; blastocyst stage: 1.7 ± 0.9% SD versus 1.9 ± 0.6% SD, respectively).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference, with data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cleavage stage or blastocyst biopsy are preferable over second polar body biopsy for determining mtDNA carryover levels in preimplantation embryos.
source: These experiments demonstrate that cleavage stage or blastocyst biopsy are preferable over biopsy of second polar bodies as methods for determining the mtDNA carryover levels found in preimplantation embryos.
evidence: Based on the finding that polar bodies have significantly higher heteroplasmy than embryos, while blastomere/TE biopsies are representative.

claim: Most mitochondria transferred with the spindle are expelled into the second polar body at the completion of meiosis II.
source: The results also suggest that while some mitochondria remain associated with the meiotic spindle, and are unavoidably transferred to the recipient cytoplast, the vast majority of these organelles do not persist into later developmental stages, with most being expelled into the second polar body at the completion of meiosis II.
evidence: Inference based on higher heteroplasmy in polar bodies compared to embryos.

claim: All parental MST mice (F1) were fertile and produced a total of 78 pups with a mean litter size of 7.8 ± 1.4 pups/animal.
source: All parental MST mice (F1) were fertile and produced a total of 78 pups, with a mean litter size of 7.8 ± 1.4 pups/animal and no significant deviations in the expected male-female ratio (59% and 41% respectively, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Fertility data from breeding experiments shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: F1 MST mice showed no significant deviations in the expected male-female ratio (59% and 41% respectively).
source: All parental MST mice (F1) were fertile and produced a total of 78 pups, with a mean litter size of 7.8 ± 1.4 pups/animal and no significant deviations in the expected male-female ratio (59% and 41% respectively, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Gender ratio data from offspring shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: All F2 pups were born alive, respired normally and grew to adulthood without manifesting any physiological or behavioral alteration.
source: All pups (F2) were born alive, respired normally and grew to adulthood without manifesting any physiological or behavioral alteration.
evidence: Observational data from F2 generation follow-up.

claim: F2-F5 mice displayed normal fertility and produced viable offspring without alterations in the expected gender ratio.
source: The fertility of these mice was assessed for a total of 5 generations, by selecting random males and females from litters (n = 9 in F2 and n = 4 between F3 and F5). Similarly, these mice also displayed normal fertility and produced viable offspring, without alterations in the expected gender ratio (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Multi-generational fertility data shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: In 239 mice analyzed by gross necropsy, all organs showed normal size, texture and morphological appearance.
source: In the 239 mice analyzed, all organs showed a normal size, texture and morphological appearance.
evidence: Gross necropsy observations from 239 mice across 5 generations.

claim: Histopathological examinations of F1 MST mice showed no lesions or visible abnormalities except for a pericardium focal inflammation in one B6 control animal.
source: Reproductive systems and accessory glands of both males (testis, epididymis, seminal vesicles, prostate, coagulating glands, ampullary glands and bulbourethral glands) and females (ovaries, oviducts, uterine horns) were also assessed. Except for a pericardium focal inflammation in one animal of the B6 control group, none of the animals showed any lesions or visible abnormalities (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Histological analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The mean heteroplasmy level in F1 mice was 2.3 ± 1.3% ranging from undetectable to 3.5% in individual mice.
source: A total of six mice (four male and two female) from F1 were sacrificed at adult age (12 weeks old). The mean heteroplasmy level in this group of mice was low at 2.3 ± 1.3% (mean ± SD, n = 6) ranging from mean frequencies of undetectable values to 3.5% in individual mice (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Heteroplasmy quantification data shown in Figure 4a and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Heteroplasmy levels were similar among different tissue types from the same mouse in F1 generation.
source: Moreover, heteroplasmy levels were similar among different tissue types from the same mouse (Figure 4b) and showed no differences between males and females.
evidence: Tissue-specific heteroplasmy data shown in Figure 4b with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA p>0.05).

claim: Heteroplasmy levels showed no differences between males and females in F1 generation.
source: Moreover, heteroplasmy levels were similar among different tissue types from the same mouse (Figure 4b) and showed no differences between males and females.
evidence: Comparison of heteroplasmy data between male and female F1 mice shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Heteroplasmy levels in F2 mice were reduced to 0.4 ± 0.6% on average.
source: Finally, the fate of the heteroplasmy was examined in adult mice derived from the MST female lineage. Four mice (two males and two females) were selected at random from each litter, through five generations. Mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy levels were reduced to 0.4 ± 0.6% (mean ± SD, n = 4) on average in F2 mice (Figure 4c and Supplementary file 5) and decreased to undetected levels in subsequent generations (F3 to F5, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Heteroplasmy quantification in F2 generation shown in Figure 4c and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Heteroplasmy decreased to undetected levels in F3 to F5 generations.
source: Mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy levels were reduced to 0.4 ± 0.6% (mean ± SD, n = 4) on average in F2 mice (Figure 4c and Supplementary file 5) and decreased to undetected levels in subsequent generations (F3 to F5, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Heteroplasmy data from F3-F5 generations shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Low levels of mtDNA heteroplasmy resultant from MST typically result in a homoplasmic state in offspring within a few generations without reversion.
source: These results suggest that low levels of mtDNA heteroplasmy resultant from MST typically result in a homoplasmic state in offspring within a few generations, without reversion (Supplementary files 5 and 6).
evidence: Based on multi-generational heteroplasmy data showing progressive reduction to undetectable levels, shown in Supplementary files 5 and 6.

claim: Different mtDNA haplogroups or mtDNA genomes affected by specific mutations might have differences in replication efficiency, influencing the speed at which homoplasmy is attained and the risk of reversion.
source: However, it is acknowledged that different mtDNA haplogroups or mtDNA genomes affected by specific mutations might have differences in the efficiency with which they replicate, influencing the speed at which homoplasmy is attained as well as the risk if reversion.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation based on known biological principles about mtDNA replication.

claim: Infertility disorders affect millions of couples worldwide.
source: Infertility disorders are a growing problem that affects millions of couples worldwide (WHO, 2017).
evidence: Cited from WHO 2017 report.

claim: Conventional IVF treatment continues to fail a significant percentage of infertile women.
source: Although assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) have evolved and can now successfully address many challenging cases (Huang and Rosenwaks, 2014; Niederberger et al., 2018), conventional IVF treatment continues to fail a significant percentage of infertile women, with many ultimately ending-up being enrolled in egg donation programs (Lutjen et al., 1984; Sauer et al., 1990; Trounson et al., 1983).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to multiple studies on IVF outcomes and egg donation.

claim: The use of donated oocytes is effective at significantly improving the chances of successful IVF treatment.
source: The use of donated oocytes is effective at significantly improving the chances of successful IVF treatment, however, the resultant children are not genetically related to the intended-mothers.
evidence: Based on established clinical practice and outcomes, implied by citations to egg donation programs.

claim: Children resulting from donated oocytes are not genetically related to the intended-mothers.
source: The use of donated oocytes is effective at significantly improving the chances of successful IVF treatment, however, the resultant children are not genetically related to the intended-mothers.
evidence: Basic biological fact about oocyte donation.

claim: Oocyte quality is defined as the competence of the oocyte to develop into a chromosomally normal blastocyst with potential to sustain a pregnancy up to a healthy live birth.
source: Oocyte quality is defined as the competence of the oocyte to develop into a chromosomally normal blastocyst with potential to sustain a pregnancy up to a healthy live birth.
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript based on established understanding in the field.

claim: Poor quality oocytes frequently fail to fertilize or produce embryos that arrest during the first stages of development.
source: Frequently, poor quality oocytes fail to fertilize or produce embryos that arrest during the first stages of development (Hardy et al., 2001; Meskhi and Seif, 2006; Pellicer et al., 1995) either due to nuclear or cytoplasmic defects (Conti and Franciosi, 2018; Eppig, 1996; Liu and Keefe, 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on oocyte quality and embryo development.

claim: Aberrant meiosis or early developmental failure is caused mainly by deficiencies in the oocyte cytoplasmic machinery.
source: Accumulated evidence suggests that aberrant meiosis or early developmental failure is caused mainly by deficiencies in the oocyte cytoplasmic machinery (Hoffmann et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2003; Liu et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2000; Liu and Keefe, 2007; Reader et al., 2017), which contains a vast diversity of critical components, including organelles, mRNAs, proteins, ribosomes and many other factors (Bianchi et al., 2015; Sathananthan, 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on oocyte cytoplasm and development.

claim: Mitochondria are the most numerous organelles in the cytoplasm.
source: Mitochondria are the most numerous organelles in the cytoplasm and play an essential role by supplying the ATP needed for the oocyte to support critical events, such as: maturation, spindle formation and segregation of chromosomes and chromatids (Chappel, 2013; May-Panloup et al., 2007).
evidence: Established biological fact supported by citations.

claim: Mitochondria play an essential role by supplying ATP needed for oocyte maturation, spindle formation and segregation of chromosomes and chromatids.
source: Mitochondria are the most numerous organelles in the cytoplasm and play an essential role by supplying the ATP needed for the oocyte to support critical events, such as: maturation, spindle formation and segregation of chromosomes and chromatids (Chappel, 2013; May-Panloup et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mitochondrial function in oocytes.

claim: Dysfunctions at the mitochondrial level and deficiencies affecting other cytoplasmic factors have been correlated with inadequate oocyte developmental competence.
source: Dysfunctions at the mitochondrial level and deficiencies affecting other cytoplasmic factors have been correlated with inadequate oocyte developmental competence (Eichenlaub-Ritter, 2012; Liu et al., 2002; Van Blerkom, 2011; Van Blerkom et al., 1995), particularly in older infertile patients (Babayev and Seli, 2015; Fragouli et al., 2015; Igarashi et al., 2016; Wells, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies correlating mitochondrial dysfunction with oocyte quality.

claim: Cytoplasmic transfer and injection of purified mitochondria have been proposed as potential methods to restore viability of compromised oocytes.
source: Techniques like cytoplasmic transfer (Cohen et al., 1998; Lanzendorf et al., 1999) or the injection of purified mitochondria (Fakih MHSM et al., 2015; Kristensen et al., 2017 have been proposed as potential methods to restore the viability of compromised oocytes in IVF patients with a history of poor embryo development or repeated implantation failures with conventional treatments.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies proposing these techniques.

claim: Live births have been reported following cytoplasmic transfer and mitochondrial injection techniques.
source: Although live births have been reported following the use of these techniques (Cohen et al., 1998; Fakih MHSM et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1999; Lanzendorf et al., 1999) their safety and/or benefits to treat infertility has been questioned.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical reports.

claim: The safety and/or benefits of cytoplasmic transfer and mitochondrial injection to treat infertility has been questioned.
source: Although live births have been reported following the use of these techniques (Cohen et al., 1998; Fakih MHSM et al., 2015; Huang et al., 1999; Lanzendorf et al., 1999) their safety and/or benefits to treat infertility has been questioned.
evidence: General statement about scientific controversy in the field.

claim: Cytoplasmic transfer experiments were abandoned due to concerns that heteroplasmy might have negative clinical consequences.
source: Cytoplasmic transfer experiments were abandoned due to concerns that heteroplasmy (i.e., the co-existence of two distinct mtDNA genomes) might have negative clinical consequences (Darbandi et al., 2017; Isasi et al., 2016; Kristensen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies discussing concerns about heteroplasmy.

claim: A recent randomized clinical study using mitochondria derived from autologous oogonial stem cells failed to demonstrate improvements in embryo developmental or clinical outcomes.
source: However, the source and quality of the mitochondria used are unclear and a recent randomized clinical study conducted using mitochondria derived from autologous oogonial stem cells failed to demonstrate improvements in embryo developmental or clinical outcomes (Labarta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Labarta et al., 2019 clinical study.

claim: Current data from human clinical research do not support the notion that addition of mitochondria from the same individual is capable of correcting cytoplasmic deficiencies in poor quality oocytes.
source: Thus, current data from human clinical research do not support the notion that the addition of further mitochondria derived from the same individual is capable of correcting cytoplasmic deficiencies (mitochondria or other) that may be present in poor quality oocytes.
evidence: Based on the negative results from clinical studies cited, particularly Labarta et al., 2019.

claim: A recent study suggested that autologous mitochondrial supplementation may induce a phenotypic effect in the heart of resultant mice.
source: Of note, a recent study suggested that autologous mitochondrial supplementation may induce a phenotypic effect in the heart of resultant mice (St John et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to St John et al., 2019.

claim: Mitochondrial replacement techniques (MRTs) were originally proposed to prevent the transmission of inherited mitochondrial diseases.
source: These techniques, known globally as mitochondrial replacement techniques (MRTs) were originally proposed to prevent the transmission of inherited mitochondrial diseases (Craven et al., 2010; Hyslop et al., 2016; Paull et al., 2013; Tachibana et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational MRT studies.

claim: A clinical application of MST to prevent transmission of Leigh Syndrome was recently reported, resulting in the birth of an unaffected child.
source: Indeed, a clinical application of maternal spindle transfer (MST) to prevent the transmission of Leigh Syndrome was recently reported, resulting the birth of an unaffected child (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2017 clinical case report.

claim: The potential of MRTs to overcome infertility remains unclear.
source: However, the potential of MRTs to overcome infertility remains unclear, as most studies utilizing this approach have not had this as their main focus, instead concentrating on their potential to avoid mitochondrial diseases; examination of nuclear-cytoplasmic interactions in oocytes and zygotes (Liu and Keefe, 2004; Liu and Keefe, 2007); the origin of female aneuploidies Palermo et al., 2002; or the decreased developmental capability of aged oocytes in animal models (Yamada and Egli, 2017).
evidence: Based on review of existing literature with citations showing focus on other applications.

claim: The NZB strain presents poor reproductive performance.
source: Firstly, NZB mice present a poor reproductive performance (Fernandes et al., 1973; Hansen CT and Whitney, 1973) and, secondly, the genetic background of the NZB strain has diverged genetically from most other mouse laboratory strains, including the hybrid B6CBAF1 strain, accompanied by characteristic differences in mtDNA sequences (Bielschowsky and Goodall, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on NZB mouse characteristics.

claim: The genetic background of the NZB strain has diverged genetically from most other mouse laboratory strains, including B6CBAF1, with characteristic differences in mtDNA sequences.
source: Firstly, NZB mice present a poor reproductive performance (Fernandes et al., 1973; Hansen CT and Whitney, 1973) and, secondly, the genetic background of the NZB strain has diverged genetically from most other mouse laboratory strains, including the hybrid B6CBAF1 strain, accompanied by characteristic differences in mtDNA sequences (Bielschowsky and Goodall, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bielschowsky and Goodall, 1970.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in the divergent mtDNA of the NZB strain provide an opportunity to evaluate carryover of organelles and resultant heteroplasmy induced by MST.
source: Additionally, single nucleotide polymorphisms in the divergent mtDNA of the NZB strain provides an opportunity to evaluate the carryover of organelles and resultant heteroplasmy induced by MST procedures (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Explanation of experimental design rationale based on genetic differences.

claim: There are conflicting reports regarding the dynamics of mtDNA heteroplasmy during the lifetime of an individual, between organs or during in vitro culture of ESCs.
source: There are conflicting reports regarding the dynamics of mtDNA heteroplasmy during the lifetime of an individual, between organs or even during in vitro culture when ESCs have been derived from MRT embryos with heteroplasmic mtDNA (Hyslop et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2016; Paull et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing conflicting results.

claim: It is unclear to what extent divergent mtDNA haplotypes in heteroplasmic organisms might lead to functional incompatibility.
source: It is also unclear to what extent divergent mtDNA haplotypes in heteroplasmic organisms might lead to functional incompatibility, either between the two types of mitochondria or between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.
evidence: Statement of uncertainty in the field based on existing knowledge gaps.

claim: Cells biopsied from MST embryos at morula or blastocyst stages present minimal levels of heteroplasmy (<2.9% mtDNA from the spindle donor).
source: This study confirms that cells biopsied from MST embryos at the morula or blastocyst stages present minimal levels of heteroplasmy (<2.9% mtDNA from the spindle donor) and that these biopsy specimens are representative of the remainder of the embryo.
evidence: Based on sequencing data from biopsied cells and corresponding embryos shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Biopsy specimens from morula or blastocyst stages are representative of the remainder of the embryo for heteroplasmy assessment.
source: This study confirms that cells biopsied from MST embryos at the morula or blastocyst stages present minimal levels of heteroplasmy (<2.9% mtDNA from the spindle donor) and that these biopsy specimens are representative of the remainder of the embryo.
evidence: Based on lack of significant difference between biopsy and whole embryo heteroplasmy levels shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Heteroplasmy levels in TE cells are more closely correlated with levels in the blastocyst as a whole or corresponding ESCs compared to second polar bodies.
source: This agrees with data from Neupane and colleagues, who have shown that, in comparison to second polar bodies, mtDNA heteroplasmy in TE cells is more closely correlated with the levels in the blastocyst as a whole or the corresponding ESCs (Neupane et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neupane et al., 2014.

claim: Oocytes might be actively removing mitochondria transferred along with the spindle because they may be disadvantageous compared to the recipient's own organelles.
source: Alternatively, oocytes might be actively removing mitochondria transferred along with the spindle, since they may be disadvantageous as compared to the recipient's own organelles (De Fanti et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to De Fanti et al., 2017.

claim: Testing of blastomeres or TE biopsies is preferable to second polar body analysis for quantification of mtDNA heteroplasmy levels.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanism, our data suggest that testing of blastomeres or TE biopsies is preferable to second polar body analysis for the quantification of mtDNA heteroplasmy levels.
evidence: Based on data showing polar bodies have higher and non-representative heteroplasmy levels.

claim: This finding has relevance for preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) of mitochondrial disease in humans.
source: This also has relevance for the preimplantation genetic testing (PGT, also known as preimplantation genetic diagnosis – PGD) of mitochondrial disease in the human.
evidence: Inference about clinical application based on the biopsy comparison data.

claim: Previous studies in monkeys and humans have shown that a minimal number of donor mitochondria are transferred using MRT (below 1–2%).
source: Previous studies in monkeys and humans have shown that a minimal number of donor mitochondria are transferred using MRT (below 1–2%) (Craven et al., 2010; Hyslop et al., 2016; Paull et al., 2013; Tachibana et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple MRT studies in primates and humans.

claim: The meiotic spindle in mouse oocytes is much larger than that of the human.
source: Nevertheless, since the meiotic spindle in mouse oocytes is much larger than that of the human, and given that multiple mitochondria are found in the vicinity of the spindle, it was expected that MST in mice would lead to higher mtDNA carryover levels.
evidence: Established biological fact about species differences.

claim: Multiple mitochondria are found in the vicinity of the spindle in mouse oocytes.
source: Nevertheless, since the meiotic spindle in mouse oocytes is much larger than that of the human, and given that multiple mitochondria are found in the vicinity of the spindle, it was expected that MST in mice would lead to higher mtDNA carryover levels.
evidence: Biological observation about mitochondrial distribution in oocytes.

claim: The low heteroplasmic levels achieved can be attributed to the use of birefringence microscopy during enucleation, which assists in minimizing carryover of cytoplasm transferred along the meiotic spindle.
source: The surprisingly low heteroplasmic levels achieved during this study can likely be attributed to the use of birefringence microscopy during enucleation, which assists in minimizing the carryover of cytoplasm transferred along the meiotic spindle.
evidence: Inference about technical factor contributing to low heteroplasmy based on methodology used.

claim: It has been suggested that organs with high-metabolic demand tend to accumulate higher heteroplasmy mtDNA levels.
source: It has also been suggested that organs with a high-metabolic demand tend to accumulate higher heteroplasmy mtDNA levels (Jenuth et al., 1997; Meirelles and Smith, 1997), however, our data do not confirm this observation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jenuth et al., 1997 and Meirelles and Smith, 1997.

claim: The current study's data do not confirm that organs with high-metabolic demand accumulate higher heteroplasmy levels.
source: It has also been suggested that organs with a high-metabolic demand tend to accumulate higher heteroplasmy mtDNA levels (Jenuth et al., 1997; Meirelles and Smith, 1997), however, our data do not confirm this observation.
evidence: Based on Figure 4b showing similar heteroplasmy across different organs including high-metabolic ones.

claim: Differences in mitochondrial haplotypes from mouse strains used could have differential replication rates, explaining the lack of organ-specific heteroplasmy accumulation.
source: This result could be explained by differences in mitochondrial haplotypes from mouse strains used, which could have a differential replication rate.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed results.

claim: Some studies of heteroplasmic ESC lines derived from embryos carrying mtDNA mutations have shown changes in levels of normal and mutant mtDNA during prolonged in vitro culture, with reversion to mutant mtDNA predominance.
source: Some studies of heteroplasmic ESC lines derived from embryos carrying mtDNA mutations have shown changes in the levels of normal and mutant mtDNA during prolonged in vitro culture, with reversion back to a situation where mutant mtDNA predominates (Hyslop et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2016; Paull et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ESC heteroplasmy dynamics.

claim: Reversion of heteroplasmy in ESCs delayed efforts for direct clinical application of MRT-derived techniques and raises concerns for the first baby born using MST.
source: This delayed efforts for the direct application of MRT-derived techniques in the clinical setting and raises some concerns for the first baby born using MST (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about impact of ESC reversion findings on clinical translation, with citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: The mechanism of heteroplasmy reversion seen in ESCs in vitro might not necessarily represent the in vivo process.
source: Nevertheless, the results presented here show a low level of mtDNA carryover in all adult organs analyzed, suggesting that the mechanism seen in ESCs in vitro might not necessarily represent the in vivo process.
evidence: Inference based on contrast between ESC culture results and in vivo data from this study.

claim: The current results agree with Sharpley et al., who showed that NZB and 129S6 mtDNA heteroplasmic haplotypes decrease over generations.
source: The results also agree with Sharpley et al, who showed that NZB and 129S6 mtDNA heteroplasmic haplotypes decrease over generations (Sharpley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharpley et al., 2012 showing similar findings.

claim: Heteroplasmy resultant from MST can be stable within an individual.
source: The data collected from the analyzed organs suggests that heteroplasmy resultant from MST can be stable within an individual and can lead to an homoplasmic state within a few generations.
evidence: Based on similar heteroplasmy levels across organs within F1 mice shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Heteroplasmy resultant from MST can lead to a homoplasmic state within a few generations.
source: The data collected from the analyzed organs suggests that heteroplasmy resultant from MST can be stable within an individual and can lead to an homoplasmic state within a few generations.
evidence: Based on progressive reduction of heteroplasmy across generations shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary files 5-6.

claim: NZB/OlaHsd mice are expected to have small litter sizes (3.8 at weaning) based on literature.
source: This is a notable observation, as based on the literature, NZB/OlaHsd mice are expected to have small litter sizes (3.8 at weaning) (Fernandes et al., 1973; Hansen CT and Whitney, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on NZB reproductive characteristics.

claim: MST mice showed good fertility with average of 7.8 pups per litter, which is notably higher than expected for NZB strain.
source: On the other hand, the MST mice followed over five generations were apparently normal and showed good fertility (average of 7.8 pups per litter). This is a notable observation, as based on the literature, NZB/OlaHsd mice are expected to have small litter sizes (3.8 at weaning) (Fernandes et al., 1973; Hansen CT and Whitney, 1973).
evidence: Comparison between observed MST fertility (7.8) and expected NZB fertility (3.8) from literature.

claim: MST can overcome a severe developmental arrest phenotype associated with poor fertility and greatly reduced chances of pregnancy following in vitro fertilization.
source: In conclusion, this study has demonstrated that MST can overcome a severe developmental arrest phenotype, associated with poor fertility and greatly reduced chances of an individual oocyte producing a pregnancy following in vitro fertilization.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental results showing rescue of NZB developmental arrest.

claim: Embryos produced using optimized MST techniques can give rise to apparently normal and fertile animals.
source: The results show that embryos produced using optimized MST techniques can give rise to apparently normal and fertile animals.
evidence: Based on health, histology, and fertility data from F1-F5 generations.

claim: Levels of heteroplasmy were low in the initial generation and undetectable in subsequent generations, indicating that homoplasmy for the mtDNA of the cytoplast donor is rapidly attained in this model.
source: Levels of heteroplasmy were low in the initial generation and undetectable in subsequent generations, indicating that homoplasmy for the mtDNA of the cytoplast donor is rapidly attained in this model.
evidence: Based on heteroplasmy data across generations shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary files 5-6.

claim: A high proportion of IVF cycles are unsuccessful due to poor embryo development related to low oocyte quality.
source: Given the high proportion of IVF cycles which are unsuccessful due to poor embryo development related to low oocyte quality, we believe that there is a need to further explore the potential of MST as a clinical treatment for infertility.
evidence: General statement about IVF outcomes based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Pre-clinical and clinical trials involving human oocytes are desirable to explore MST as a therapy for infertility.
source: Pre-clinical and clinical trials involving human oocytes, undertaken in a regulated and carefully controlled manner, is desirable, since such a therapy could represent the last chance for infertile patients to have genetically related children.
evidence: Recommendation based on the positive results from this study.

claim: MST therapy could represent the last chance for infertile patients to have genetically related children.
source: Pre-clinical and clinical trials involving human oocytes, undertaken in a regulated and carefully controlled manner, is desirable, since such a therapy could represent the last chance for infertile patients to have genetically related children.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical application.
